items.title: A failure to deliver, not a rejection of the right
paras: There is no running from it: the results for Republicans in the 2026 midterms were bad. Really bad.

Democrats will now control both the House of Representatives and the Senate with handy majorities and have already indicated their oversight powers will be used to go after officials within the Trump Administration. Democrats managed this feat, despite a majority of Americans holding an unfavourable view of their party.
Across the United States, decades-old voting patterns were upended, with support for Republicans disappearing, even in areas that had long been considered safe.
Nowhere was that more apparent than in the two major hubs of American conservatism: Texas and Florida.
Not since the Reagan Administration has Texas elected a Democrat to the Senate, yet State Representative James Talarico defeated Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton with ease.

Paxton, a man who had been impeached by his fellow Republicans in the Texas Legislature and admitted to an extramarital affair with a GOP staffer, had toppled four-term incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the primaries off the back of a Trump endorsement.
Even the President’s home state of Florida, a real stronghold for Republicans in recent years, produced races which were far closer than expected.
These midterm results were undoubtedly a rebuke of the Trump Administration. Deservedly so.
But it is critically important that we don’t misdiagnose what occurred here.
Voters had been promised the ‘Golden Age of America’. They were told, in the typical populist fashion, that their concerns were being ignored by the political establishment.

President Trump first won the keys to the White House with this very message: politicians of all stripes have become entrenched in the DC ‘swamp’, wrapped up with donors and lobbyists, and they have failed to deliver for everyday Americans.

In 2024, he explicitly promised that prices would come down and that Americans wouldn’t be sent to die in yet another protracted Middle Eastern war. It was promises like these that Trump’s coalition of supporters clung on to, turning out in massive numbers to vote for in 2024.
When populist governments fail to deliver on their promised agendas, they are acutely vulnerable to a strong reaction from voters.
After all, why vote for a populist alternative like MAGA if they produce outcomes scarcely different to that of the traditional political establishment?
Without offering an endorsement of his more extreme methods, a prime example of the virtues of delivery for a populist government is President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador.

Bukele has taken the Latin American nation from one of the homicide and gang violence hotspots of the world to a state of relative security in a very short span of time. The Salvadoran President promised to end gang violence, and he has been rewarded for delivering, enjoying an average approval rating in the high 80s across his presidency and being re-elected with 84.65 per cent of the vote in 2024.

Shifting focus back stateside, according to the New York Times, young men had a swing of nearly 40 points towards the Democrats in the midterms, just two years after shifting towards Trump by 23 points.

The US-Israeli war in Iran was seen as a betrayal of them and of millions of other Americans who placed their faith in a second Trump presidency. Twenty-three US military personnel have died since the conflict began in February, and what exactly does this administration have to show for it?
The devastating effects the Iran conflict has had on the global economy, particularly on the oil supply, have been felt acutely in the communities which had supported Trump most strongly.
They made their voices heard loudly, and they can’t afford to be ignored now.

One small consolation that the GOP can take from the midterms is that immigration remains an area of relative strength. In exit polling, immigration appeared as virtually the only issue that voters rated Republicans higher than Democrats on. The Democratic media strategy also gives credence to this, with the focus largely placed on the cost of living and tying it to the war in Iran, rather than the ICE raids seen in cities across the country.
This may indicate that, for better or for worse, the Trump Administration is seen to be delivering on its immigration agenda.

I do concede that some within the DC establishment may still attempt to use this enormous election defeat to push for a softer approach to immigration. The President himself even appeared to signal a backtrack, acknowledging in a recent 60 Minutes interview that perhaps his crackdown on immigration was ‘too tough’. However, backing down on this issue would invariably be seen as yet another broken promise to increasingly disillusioned voters.
Immigration is still fertile ground for the Republicans and must remain on their agenda for the next election.

In a similar way, plenty of conservative measures which were voted on in referenda at the state level were successful, even in states where Republican candidates fared badly. Nevada, North Carolina, and Ohio all voted overwhelmingly for voter ID, while in Arizona and Colorado, measures that protect women’s-only spaces and ban transgender surgery for children passed as well.
This certainly suggests that it wasn’t conservatism, nationalism, or the political right being rejected by voters this election; it was the failures of the Trump GOP.

Attention must now turn to the future of the Republican Party, and of course, the nominee for 2028. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have long been touted as successors to Trump, but are they not also complicit in this historic disaster?
Could the hawkish Rubio really be expected to regain trust from war-weary voters? Can the sitting Vice President really extricate himself from the baggage of this administration?
Have either of them really earned the right to carry the flag? At this stage, the answer is a definitive no.
In the aftermath of this loss, Vice President Vance put out a post on X outlining four main areas of dissatisfaction:

While Vance himself may be too close to these decisions to avoid culpability, his instinct in diagnosing the issues that turned voters away is sound. They can provide a roadmap for a successful candidate in two years’ time.
Also on X, the Young Republicans of Texas revealed they had received a slew of new applications to join their ranks, even after Texas saw the worst result for Republicans in decades.

Many young Americans may have abandoned the GOP at this election, but this is a sign that they are not abandoning the field entirely. If you simply deliver what they voted for two years ago, that support can be regained.

Therein lies the hope for the next presidential election. End the war in Iran and avoid further entanglements, bring down costs, push ahead with action on immigration, and above all, put America first.
If these are the battlelines that are drawn, a worthwhile candidate can sweep the 2028 primaries and regain the voters that abandoned the GOP.
Heed the lessons of this brutal wake-up call and in two years’ time, the Republicans can win the White House.
Kieran Phillips works within Queensland politics and has an academic background in international relations, with particular interests in political theory and foreign affairs.

items.title: Father Christmas greeted by estimated 335,000 at Adelaide pageant
paras: Father Christmas's annual arrival in Adelaide was met with adoration. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
Thousands have lined the streets for the Adelaide Christmas Pageant, marking the start of the festive season in the city.
Pageant-goers flocked to the city early to secure good spots, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas.
While the David Jones collapse has left a cloud over the Magic Cave, the popular Christmas attraction remains open.
More than 300,000 people are estimated to have lined the streets for this year's Adelaide Christmas Pageant, the 94th edition of the annual yuletide parade.
Pageant-goers arrived in the city early, along with hundreds of performers who gathered near South Terrace and King William Road, ahead of the much-loved parade.
Young faces lined the CBD streets to watch the floats pass by, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
Five new floats were added to this year's line-up, including The Magic Hat and A Bumper Christmas.
"Seeing all the floats go past, they love it," one parent said while sitting with his family.
Hundreds of performers took part in the event. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
Organisers believe about 335,000 people turned out for the event, which culminated with the much-anticipated arrival of Father Christmas.

Beneath grey skies, a slight shadow was cast on proceedings by the collapse of David Jones, whose Adelaide store has hosted the children's Christmas attraction, the Magic Cave, for almost three decades, although it will continue operating for the time being.
But, overwhelmingly, there were beaming smiles along the event's route.
Five new floats were added to this year's line-up. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
Renowned children's entertainer Emma Watkins, better known by her stage name Emma Memma, said she was thrilled to be back after making her debut last year.
This year Watkins was part of the float The Sounds and Signs of Christmas, a reference to her push to help make entertainment more accessible for deaf and and hearing children alike.
Emma Memma says she is thrilled to be back for the Christmas Pageant. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )
"Today is the first time that my co-performer Elvin Lam is actually joining me in the pageant," she said.
"It's his first Christmas pageant ever, and Elvin is profoundly deaf, and he will be signing throughout the whole parade."
Kunal Dhingra and his family were among those who rose early to secure good spots.
"I can see a lot of people are here from different backgrounds. All the kids are really happy," he said while holding his slightly tired infant daughter.
Kunal Dhingra and his family were among the early risers. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
A cross-section of the community was present at the time-honoured parade, with young pageant-goer Miabelle saying she relished "spending time with my cousins" and seeing the floats.
Another attendee, a local grandmother, said her connection to the event went back decades.
The event brings Christmas magic to the streets of Adelaide. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
The Magic Cave, held in David Jones at the Adelaide Central Plaza, has been part of the city's Christmas landscape since 1998 when its original host John Martin's closed down.
While the Magic Cave welcomed Father Christmas this year, questions have emerged about what lies ahead for the attraction.
Last week, David Jones went into voluntary administration, with 19 of its 38 stores slated for closure across Australia and New Zealand.
Organisers estimate more than 300,000 people attended. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )
In SA, stores in Westfield Marion and Westfield West Lakes will shut down by the end of the year.
But the store in Rundle Mall will remain open, and locals are keen to keep the Magic Cave as part of Adelaide's Christmas festivities.
"It's an Adelaide icon, bringing my now baby like when I was a kid, and now letting her do it," local woman Erin said.
"We need David Jones … we need the Magic Cave, the kids love it, it's one thing they look forward to."
Entertainers were everywhere to be seen on the city's streets. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke )

items.title: Silence on coal, hubris at Cop31
paras: Anthony Albanese strutted out onto the Cop31 stage to crow about climate change. Cop31 is a place where the alpha roosters have been locked up so the weak beta- bantams can strut their stuff. If they were serious about reducing emissions, nuclear energy would be front and centre. If Albanese was serious about addressing the global boiling nonsense, he would have shut down coal. But he didn’t mention the word.

The official transcript of Albanese’s Cop31 Leaders’ Summit speech did not include the words ‘coal’, ‘fossil fuels’, ‘gas’, or ‘oil’. There was no reference to shutting down, phasing out, or transitioning away from coal or fossil fuels. The speech focused on Australia’s renewables growth, rooftop solar and batteries, Pacific Island vulnerability, climate finance, and the Pacific Resilience Facility.
In my opinion, Albanese is not serious about addressing climate change or carbon emissions. However, the Labor government is serious about extending the network of grifters to the Pacific and beyond.
Albanese was unable to say in his speech what Cop31 is all about – ending coal. That would be political suicide for him at home.

Meanwhile, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the quiet part out loud. He said that fossil fuels ‘must go the way of the dinosaurs’ and that ‘the dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do’. He also called for no new coal expansion and a faster transition away from fossil fuels.

Australia is the world’s largest exporter of steel-making (metallurgical) coal and the second-largest exporter of power-station (thermal) coal by volume. In 2024, roughly 362 million tonnes of coal in total were shipped overseas. This was about 24 per cent of the global seaborne coal trade.

At around US$56.5 billion, Australia earnt (and continues to earn) more from coal exports than any other country. Forecasts by the Department of Industry Resources and Energy put power-station coal exports at about 209 megatonnes in 2026-27, reducing only slightly to 199 megatonnes by 2030-31.

Steel-making coal volumes are forecast to rise slightly over the same period. Combined power-station and steel-making coal export earnings are still in the tens of billions of dollars annually and remain a major component of Australia’s resource exports.

Instead, the Labor government is funding free coffee for everyone at Cop31 to the tune of $32,000. Meanwhile, cafes in Australia are struggling to make ends meet, and ordinary Australians are struggling to pay for their daily coffee.
Albanese and Bowen know they have to tread softly with our mining sector. They risk not only upsetting Australia’s wealthiest individuals, but also the mining industry unions.

That explains why since 2022, the Albanese government has approved dozens of coal, oil, and gas projects and extensions. These are not short-term projects: the North West Shelf extension runs to 2070, and the 1,695-well Australia Pacific LNG expansion has been approved out to 2081.

Australians are probably sick of hearing about it, but the record Australian delegation of 193 officials and the $148 million budget allocation over three years for Australia’s Cop31 role, plus the roughly $2.3 million already committed for the Antalya trip is no small price to go on the world stage and say nothing.

I’ve banged on about nuclear before, but it must be said. If the goal is rapid, reliable emissions reduction, nuclear is the only technology that has actually displaced coal at scale in places like France, Sweden, and South Korea. Australia has the uranium, the geology, and the technical capacity, yet neither Albanese nor Bowen put it on the table at Cop31.
Labor’s grifting instinct is the real reason Australian taxpayers are funding the ultimate swan in Turkey. They’re taking us for geese.

Albanese has announced Australia’s $100 million contribution to the Pacific Resilience Facility. This is in addition to the pre-Cop shocker in Tuvalu and Fiji where Bowen could barely keep his eyes open. Albanese’s speech spent more time on Pacific finance and vulnerability than on the coal that still underwrites Australia’s export income.

There’s a reason for this. It allows Albanese and Bowen to pretend to be statesmen. The best Australian statesmen did so through superior intellect, diplomatic and negotiation skills, and forethought.
Albanese and Bowen do statesmanship through other people’s money. They’re running out of it at home and now they’re splashing it across the Pacific. The hubris is palpable.
Dr Michael de Percy @FlaneurPolitiq is the Spectator Australia’s Canberra Press Gallery Correspondent. If you’d like to support his writing, please shout him a drink over at Donorbox .

items.title: ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO
paras: Advertisement Business Companies Executive shake-up ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO Drake Bennett and Ian King November 14, 2026 — 4:30pm
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, his surrender was unconditional . Huang’s usual take-charge demeanour had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care”.

During the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth , Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up.

The downfall of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has been swift and unexpected. Marija Ercegovac It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigour , he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours.

It’s hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and its chips, and it’s hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company’s board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang’s ouster, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.”

When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang’s, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them.

Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He’d been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said.

A turning point came last Friday, November 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterwards, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The board announced they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company , admitting to the affair, apologising to his family and vowing to “cooperate fully” with the board’s investigation.

As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang’s attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia’s idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had about 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days, the response times had grown longer.

The Nvidia board acted fast after a reported that Huang was having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely.

The next morning, the board announced that chief financial officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try to reassure rattled employees. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. “More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The board, staff and I recognise that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.”

She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on November 18. A day earlier, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Street analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.

Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. It’s hard to imagine anyone filling all Huang’s roles – technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot – and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company, managed in a more regular way.

As for Huang himself, he won’t be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he’s expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia’s state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who’ve spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a “piece of shit” . He claims he does not care what happens to him at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination.

items.title: Newcastle climate protest goes ahead, no arrests made
paras: Rising Tide says more than 900 people registered for the paddle-out protest. ( ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy )
More than 600 kayakers took to Newcastle Harbour as part of "Paddle for the Planet", protesting coal exports.
Protest organisers and NSW Police say no arrests were made as hundreds of kayakers took to Newcastle Harbour in New South Wales, to protest against coal exports and fossil fuels.
Climate activism group Rising Tide began promoting its "Paddle for the Planet" event in August, but Newcastle Council this week moved to ban the group from holding any of its events on council land.
NSW Police attempted to block the protest, citing safety concerns and potential resourcing pressures.
However, the court dismissed the application on Friday , deciding the event was in the public interest.
The Supreme Court of NSW dismissed an application by NSW Police to stop the on-water protest. ( ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy )
Speaking after the paddle-out, Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein labelled Anthony Albanese "hypocritical", as the prime minister and climate change minister engage in the COP31 summit.
"[Albanese] is over in Türkiye telling the world that Australia is a leader in climate action, when the opposite is true," Mr Hallenstein said.
"Both Albanese's federal Labor government, and Chris Minns's state Labor government continue to approve new coal and gas projects, which is the opposite of action on climate change."
Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein spoke out at the event. ( ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy )
The event was held off Horseshoe Beach, which is managed by Transport for NSW.
A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed, by the completion of the event, officers had not made any arrests.
Organisers say more than 900 people registered for the event, with more than 600 taking to the water.
Hundreds more lined the shore of Horseshoe Beach for the hour-long demonstration.
"I'm tired of governments, from the federal government down to the local government, not doing enough about reducing [climate impact]," attendee Scott Alcorn said.
"I can see there's plenty of enthusiastic people who feel just the same way as I do."
Protesters formed a line across Newcastle's harbour during the one-hour paddle-out. ( ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy )
In the Supreme Court hearing, Assistant Commissioner David Waddell and NSW Police's legal representative argued there were serious safety concerns for large amounts of people on the water.
The Port of Newcastle did not run any shipping movements between 10am and 2pm.
NSW Greens spokesperson for climate change and justice Sue Higginson said climate change and fossil fuel projects must be a key concern in the NSW election, scheduled for March 13, 2027.
She argued while the cost of living is the biggest issue for voters coming into the campaign period, it "does not mean people are not also concerned about the health of their local environment".
"Labor and the Coalition, all they want to do is talk about One Nation … what we are doing is providing the people with a real alternative and a real vision for their future."
NSW Greens MLC Sue Higginson declared her support to the Rising Tide movement. ( ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy )
Ms Higginson also referred to a recent decision by the Minns government to make legislative changes allowing the Mount Pleasant coalmine in the Upper Hunter to increase its life and output.
The premier announced the move despite a High Court ruling relating to the mine that concluded global climate emissions must be considered in approvals.
"[The government] is literally carving laws that defy the High Court's ruling because a coal company is threatening to lay off workers before Christmas," she said.
Ms Higginson said the matter is set to be debated in NSW parliament next week.
A Rising Tide spokesperson confirmed the group plans to hold a larger on-water protest at the end of February on Newcastle Harbour, a fortnight before the election.

items.title: Reserve Bank of India imposes monetary penalty on One Mobikwik Systems Limited
paras: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 06, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹9.00 lakh (Rupees Nine Lakh only) on One Mobikwik Systems Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of the directions issued by RBI on ‘Prepaid Payment lnstruments (PPIs)’ and ‘Fraud reporting’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under the provisions of section 30(1) read with section 26(6) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its operations for the period from June 2025 to March 2026. Based on supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for its failure to comply with the said RBI directions. After considering the company’s reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: the company had allowed fund transfer by certain PPI holders to non-pre-registered beneficiaries beyond the prescribed limit. the company failed to report certain frauds within the prescribed timeline. The action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1496

items.title: Six people arrested in cross-border drugs smuggling network: ED
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network . An investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement ( ED ) unearthed a major drug trafficking operation involving the smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India. Lovejit Singh alias Labba , Manjeet Singh alias Manna were arrested on October 11 while Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh and Ramandeep Singh were arrested on October 18 and one Gurpreet Singh was held on October 20, the agency said in a statement. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons ie Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi. They were were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder.

According to the central probe agency the accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs. According to ED , the investigation under PMLA linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network was initiated based on the seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by DRI and the seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 Kg. of heroin has been seized so far. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where the identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. The accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in the local market. Further, the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles in the second-hand market for trafficking from the storage hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri Madhya Pradesh, and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Previously, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits were attached by the ED . (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. items.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives.

The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in.

I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall

I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams

I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman

1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Evans

As a pupil in the mid-1960s at a girls’ grammar school in the north of England, one day I picked up a copy of New Scientist in the library. I was mind-blown by an article about Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity and time dilation, including a coloured diagram! I went on to study physical and material sciences at university and worked for eight years in research. But motherhood and misogyny (in those days before equal opportunities legislation) led me to change tack and I’ve been making pottery by hand for over 55 years. I like to think my science education hasn’t been wasted, but handed down to my daughters, one of whom reads New Scientist online in France. Every week, the paper issue landing on my doormat is devoured with excitement! Anne Rodgers

The stories that most interested me were about emerging electronics, the Sputnik satellite and the launch of Laika the space dog. The last of these prompted me to construct a module to house a maggot atop a 3-pence standard firework rocket and launch it. I later recovered the maggot unharmed and used it as fishing bait the next day. Mel

We are a group of 12 ladies “of a certain age” who meet once a month to discuss three or four articles from New Scientist . We tackle topics such as AI, quantum computing and cosmology – all of which are quite daunting! We persevere and continue to try to understand topics like these that are very challenging. We look up terms and concepts we don’t understand and then teach each other. We also love to read articles on climate change and medical science, as these feel more relatable. We plan to get the recordings of the talks from October’s New Scientist Live , so we can watch together and discuss. We want to thank you for making science accessible to us – we all feel that it’s important as we get older to not give in to the temptation to ignore all the new discoveries and changes in the world. Diana Currie, Dawn Segrue and the Marlow Science Group

An article about Benjamin Libet’s experiments in the 1980s showing there was a time gap between the brain making a decision and conscious awareness of that decision inspired me, as a psychotherapist, to find a way of using that gap in the field of psychological therapy. Two years of exploration and testing later, I taught the first cohort of students, and now it is being employed by psychologists, counsellors, psychiatrists and psychotherapists all over the world. Terence Watts
On the eve of New Scientist’s 70th anniversary, newsroom legend Andy Coghlan reveals four of the most dramatic and surprising moments from his storied career

Back in 2019, I stumbled across an eye-catching magazine on the shelves of a Tesco store. The title-page article caught my eye: “Does this one microbe cause all these conditions… and does that mean we can beat them?” It was at that moment that I truly fell in love with biology. Years have passed, and I have since graduated with a science degree from the University of Edinburgh and am now a returning student at my alma mater pursuing a master of research postgraduate degree in life sciences.

One day, I aim to be able to contribute – even if just a little – to aiding humanity in its endless fight against malady and illness. All of my academic achievements thus far may very well not have been possible had it not been for that magazine that caught my eye, that day in August 2019. And for that, I quite literally owe New Scientist all my academic achievements, and all that I have done, to this day. Stephen Wang

I am 87 and have been reading New Scientist every week since October 1964. I still have a note from my grandson, Maximilian, from when he was 5 years old, thanking me for reading New Scientist with him. He is now studying biology at my one-time college, Merton, at the University of Oxford. In the meantime, he has already succeeded, while travelling with his mother in Amazonia, in identifying, describing, naming and publishing a new genus and species of damselfly. He and I continue to discuss issues like evolution together, though I am a classicist by training. Anthony J. Nieduszynski

Your magazine is vital to our family. It sparks many conversations at the kitchen table. Our 11-year-old grandson keeps beating us to the latest issue. Our 6-year-old grandson has been enthralled with the cover art since he was 3. I cut out the cartoons and post them on the fridge. They have become the “cartoon of the week”. Often my grandsons see details I didn’t even catch. Krystyna Rodriguez
From subconscious finger sniffing to rats driving cars, New Scientist staff have reported on many weird, wild or utterly bonkers discoveries and inventions in the 70 years since we began

I have been a reader for almost all the publication’s life, as I first started when I was studying for A level qualifications in 1959/60. The article that really got me was one about the trouble the UK Ministry of Defence was having with dolphins that disrupted its torpedo testing by racing the torpedoes and giving them nudges of encouragement or perhaps challenge, thus putting them off target. I was hooked. It settled my decision to study engineering and, about six years later, I was actually employed as an engineer, working in a team trying to design turbine blades with better efficiency. I am now 83 and retired (well almost), but I still read every issue from cover to cover. Bryan Wilson

We first met when I was 18. I liked you a lot, but didn’t subscribe until I started my modest career as a poet of science rhymes for children (2009). Your writers, including Graham Lawton , Michael Marshall and Leah Crane , inspired 26 of the 80 poems I had published in CSIRO’s children’s science magazine Double Helix in Australia (plus many other poetic creations). In 2021, you kindly published my poem Brassica Bonanza on your Almost the last word pages (9 January), and Frosty Window Pane made it into Almost the last word in 2023 (13 May). So, I feel like we are friends now as well as work colleagues. And somewhere within that timeframe, my regular New Scientist magazine became INDISPENSABLE for more personal reasons. You have become my safe substitute for cigarettes. Every time I take a break, you help me not crave those nicotine nasties with your enlightening prose. Please don’t leave me! Love, Celia Berrell

I met my husband, Simon, on your dating website in 2012. It took me 50 years to find him, and without your mag, I probably never would have. We are two halves of a whole, and have been happily married now for 11 years. He is my heart’s delight, he makes me laugh, wears cravats with his T-shirts and is altogether quirky, like me. I still read New Scientist every week, and hope to be reading it still for many years to come. The quality of articles is outstanding – one day I may even get to understand quantum physics! We both love Tom Gauld’s cartoons , and keep a selection of them on the wall in the toilet, to entertain visitors. Andrea Cohen

I was delighted when my question about whether anything eats wasps was published in The Last Word ( 29 January 2005 ), and even more so when there was a full page of answers. But I was amazed when my question featured in the title of the first New Scientist questions book later that year. Apparently, the book was one of that Christmas’s bestsellers. Not only that, but there were two consecutive reviews in The Times – pretty good for my complete published scientific writing! And what did I get out of this? The original answerers got 25 quid each. Me? Not a penny. Only a fleeting, obscure fame. Fair enough. A great science magazine for the ordinary folks like myself. I will not be cancelling my subscription. Tom Eastwood

I answered my first two Last Word questions in 1997, when the column was relatively new. Amusingly, both appeared in the same issue, something I gather the rules now prevent. I had always admired New Scientist , but never quite imagined it would publish anything I might write – perhaps a touch of imposter syndrome. Nearly 30 years later, I’m still providing answers. I particularly enjoy questions requiring a back-of-the-envelope calculation or a little mathematical modelling. I like getting absorbed in a problem and trying to explain a tricky concept clearly and concisely. It is one of the few ways I experience mindfulness.

Some questions have spun off in unexpected directions. One, about whether pigeons sweat , led to an email while I was scuba-diving in Thailand asking me to appear on the TV programme BBC Breakfast . Answers have also developed into articles elsewhere, sometimes after reading somebody else’s answer and questioning my own. My favourite? Like the Eye of Sauron, my focus is always on the one I’m looking at right now. Mike Follows

On this day, November 14 in 1994, tennis legend Martina Navratilova , aged 38, played her final match on the tour, defeated by Gabriela Sabatini in the first round of the WTA Tour Championships (6-4, 6-2). Martina Navratilova, born in 1956 in Prague, Czechoslovakia, was, according to Billie Jean King, “the greatest singles, doubles, and mixed doubles player who ever lived”.

Since 1968, when the Open Era began, no male or female player had won more singles titles than Navratilova (167), doubles events (177), or matches (2,189). Left-handed, Navratilova played serve-and-volley unlike any woman before her.
items.impact: She only missed the mixed doubles Australian Open title to complete the Boxed Set Grand Slam, meaning winning all the four Slams in singles, doubles and mixed doubles.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
